analysis.one_liner: Bans exports of American natural gas that are meant to be shipped abroad again through foreign LNG terminals.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with no cosponsors and never came up for a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for anyone to export natural gas produced or refined in the United States when the purpose is to send that gas through an LNG (liquefied natural gas) terminal in another country for shipment onward. The bill's findings point to corruption and fuel theft in Mexico, favoritism there toward state-owned energy companies, and changes to Mexico's courts as reasons US gas should not be exported through foreign terminals. In practice, the bill would channel LNG exports through terminals located in the United States instead of ones being built abroad, such as in Mexico. The bill was introduced in September 2024, sent to the Senate Energy Committee, and never moved again before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the main beneficiaries would be companies that own or operate LNG export terminals in the United States, since exports intended for re-export through foreign terminals would have to be handled at domestic facilities instead. That protection would come at the expense of developers building LNG terminals in Mexico and of gas producers and traders who would have one fewer route for moving product to overseas buyers. The bill's stated aim is national security and trade fairness—pressuring Mexico over corruption, fuel theft, and treatment of US investors—but the binding economic effect falls on where LNG export capacity gets used.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that exporting US natural gas through foreign LNG terminals, rather than terminals in the United States, is against the national interest and a national security and trade concern.

Its findings describe corruption and fuel theft in Mexico, Mexican favoritism toward state-owned energy companies over US and Canadian investors, and judicial changes in 2024 that put Mexico's courts under political control, as reasons US gas should not flow through foreign terminals for onward shipment.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the cost would fall first on natural gas producers and traders who wanted to move US gas through foreign LNG terminals, and on companies building those terminals in Mexico, whose business model would be cut off. Consumers would be affected only indirectly; there is little in the record about effects on household energy prices either way.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gas producers and Mexican terminal builders

drawbacks.text: The bill would restrict where American natural gas can be shipped, limiting producers' access to export routes through foreign terminals and potentially affecting the price and reliability of gas sales to nearby markets.

Its ban is based on country-level judgments about corruption in Mexico, which is a trade restriction imposed on the basis of another government's conduct rather than on any safety or economic test applied to specific shipments.
No other senator cosponsored the bill, which suggests it did not build the broad backing needed to move in a Senate where most bills require agreement from many members to advance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated benefits—protecting US LNG terminal investment and pressuring Mexico over trade and corruption concerns—come with real tradeoffs: the restriction narrows where American natural gas can flow, and gas piped to a Mexican terminal before being liquefied and shipped out might, in some cases, have delivered cheaper energy to buyers than routing everything through US terminals. For ordinary Americans the bill would likely change little at the pump or the meter; the contest is mainly between competing export routes and the companies behind them. Because the bill never advanced past a single sponsor and a committee referral, no costs or benefits were actually imposed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved further before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Dan Sullivan introduced S. 5286 on September 25, 2024, near the end of the 118th Congress.
The Senate's only action on the bill was to read it twice and refer it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and bills that do not pass die when a Congress ends.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: US natural gas exporters keep their existing options, including exports routed through foreign terminals, and no new restriction was imposed. Lawmakers spent no political capital on the issue, and the US LNG terminal industry faces no added mandate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; no industry gained or lost

for.name: Sen. Dan Sullivan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its findings on Mexico's corruption, energy policies, and judicial changes; it was referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where he serves.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action—no hearing, no markup, no vote—before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no votes, so the record shows nothing about how the parties would have lined up.

industries.note: The bill would require gas intended for liquefaction and shipment abroad to be exported from domestic LNG terminals, making US terminals the mandatory channel for exports that might otherwise be handled through terminals in Mexico. The export business continues, but it stays anchored at US facilities.

industries.industry: Natural gas pipeline and terminal developers in Mexico
industries.note: The bill targets the practice of sending US gas to foreign LNG terminals for liquefaction and re-export, which would cut off the business model of Mexican terminals that depend on American pipeline gas.

Exports would still be allowed from US terminals, but the bill narrows available export routes and inserts a restriction on where US gas can be liquefied and shipped. Producers keep the export market but lose flexibility.
